title: Amazon Linux 2027 Enters Public Preview with SELinux Enforcing by Default
gist: AWS put Amazon Linux 2027 into public preview on the AL2023 baseline with SELinux in enforcing mode by default, kernel 7.1+, AWS-LC crypto and AWS Neuron accelerator drivers. The enforcing-by-default switch is the real migration cost, and AWS has published neither an AL2023 end-of-support date, a GA date, nor an in-place upgrade path.

themes.theme: SELinux enforcing as the migration cost

insights.claim: Amazon Linux 2027 ships SELinux in enforcing mode by default, whereas Amazon Linux 2023 ships it in permissive mode where policy violations are logged rather than blocked.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Every AWS-hosted workload on AL2023 now carries an undocumented compliance debt that surfaces only at OS upgrade time — budget test cycles, not just AMI swaps.
insights.locator: SELinux enforcing is the operational difference.

insights.claim: Applications that run fine today only because SELinux merely complained about their behavior will fail outright on the new Amazon Linux release unless their file contexts, ports and access patterns match policy.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Failure mode is silent until upgrade; ops teams running legacy in-house apps on AWS face an unbudgeted remediation wave.
insights.locator: Applications that run on AL2023 because SELinux only complained

insights.claim: The most valuable use of the public preview is validating workloads against SELinux enforcing rather than benchmarking the new kernel.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals where the real engineering hours go in an AWS OS refresh cycle — security policy conformance, not performance tuning.
insights.locator: For teams evaluating the preview, the practical work is testing

insights.claim: The Amazon Linux 2027 announcement states neither when AL2023 support ends nor when the new version reaches general availability.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Absence of an EOL date blocks enterprise migration planning and typically delays adoption by quarters.
insights.locator: the announcement does not say when AL2023 support ends

insights.claim: AWS principal engineer Benjamin Herrenschmidt said in a LinkedIn discussion that the kernel will keep being updated until it reaches LTS, making the previewed 7.1 a starting point rather than the version shipped at general availability.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Kernel-version-sensitive testing done now against the preview may not carry over to GA — discount preview validation work accordingly.
insights.locator: The kernel version is not settled.

insights.claim: Preview coverage is deliberately partial: AMIs are in all commercial regions in x86-64 and ARM variants and container base images are on the Amazon ECR Public Gallery, but on-premises images are not yet available because the team hit a last-minute issue.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hybrid and on-prem shops cannot start evaluation yet, further staggering adoption across the installed base.
insights.locator: Preview coverage is broad but incomplete.

themes.theme: Cattle-vs-pets and the missing upgrade path

insights.claim: The top-upvoted community question about the new Amazon Linux release was whether an in-place migration path from AL2023 exists, and it received no answer from AWS.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Practitioner demand is concentrated on migration mechanics, not features — a gap AWS has not closed and a friction point for OS refresh revenue.
insights.locator: The first question in the community response was about migration

insights.claim: The cloud-native answer that hosts are replaced rather than upgraded in place breaks down because organizations always retain some stateful 'pet' servers that cannot simply be re-provisioned.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The persistent pet-server tail is what sustains demand for migration tooling and long-tail OS support contracts.
insights.quote: I understand, but even in a world of cattle, unfortunately there are always going to be things stuck as pets.
insights.locator: Another user replied that cloud-native usage replaces hosts

insights.claim: EC2 root volume replacement was proposed as a partial migration route, but it only works for instances that keep no state on the root volume and therefore does not solve the general upgrade problem.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Partial workarounds mean migration effort stays manual and per-workload, raising the cost of each Amazon Linux generation change.
insights.locator: A third suggested EC2 root volume replacement

insights.claim: AWS's OS release cadence is running ahead of enterprise adoption, with at least one practitioner still working to move teams inside his organization onto the previous AL2023 generation as AL2027 previews.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Large installed bases lag releases by years — treat new-OS announcements as weak near-term signals of actual platform mix.
insights.locator: The gap between release cadence and adoption showed up

themes.theme: Distro trust and the RHEL-derivative comparison

insights.claim: Distrust of IBM-owned Red Hat's source availability changes — specifically fear that Rocky, Alma and Oracle will be forced to re-engineer their approach again — is cited as a reason to pick Amazon Linux instead.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Red Hat's licensing posture is actively pushing enterprise Linux share toward hyperscaler-owned distributions — watch RHEL-derivative seat migration.
insights.locator: The choice of Amazon Linux over other RHEL-derived distributions

insights.claim: Amazon Linux is characterized as analogous to Oracle Linux — controlled by a vendor users dislike but fully open source and free of the licensing strings attached to Oracle Java — rather than as a vendor lock-in play.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Lock-in fear is not the barrier to Amazon Linux adoption; differentiation is, which caps how much strategic value AWS extracts from owning the OS.
insights.quote: Owned by a terrible company, yes, but it is completely open source and genuinely is no-strings-attached, unlike Oracle Java with its restrictive license.
insights.locator: On r/linux, another placed Amazon Linux against a different comparison

insights.claim: The counterargument to AWS's cloud-optimization pitch is that Amazon Linux is a redistribution of software already available elsewhere, leaving little reason to adopt it.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: If cloud-tuning claims are not measurable, AWS's OS play is defensive plumbing rather than a moat or monetizable product line.
insights.locator: He added that there is little reason to use it

themes.theme: AI-workload positioning of the OS layer

insights.claim: Amazon Linux 2027 adds accelerator drivers including AWS Neuron support for machine learning workloads and uses AWS-LC for cryptographic operations, positioning the OS for AI/ML alongside web apps, databases and containerized microservices.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Baking Neuron drivers into the default OS lowers friction for AWS's in-house AI silicon versus Nvidia-based instances — a quiet distribution advantage for Trainium/Inferentia.
insights.locator: AL2027 runs on kernel 7.1 or later, uses AWS-LC
